[{:db/id 17592186152916 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153445 :tutorial/content "Suppose $a$ is an integer, and ${\color{red}{n}}$ is a positive integer. As we've seen, the *division algorithm* states that there exists a unique integer $q$ and a unique positive integer ${\color{blue}{r}}$ such that

$$
a = q{\color{red}{n}}+{\color{blue}{r}}, \qquad 0\leq {\color{blue}{r}} < {\color{red}{n}}.
$$

When two integers $a$ and $b$ have the *same remainder* ${\color{blue}{r}}$ when divided by ${\color{red}{n}},$ we say they are **congruent modulo** $\boldsymbol n,$ and we write

$$
a\equiv b\qquad  (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

The number $n$ is called the **modulus**.

To demonstrate this concretely, consider the following list of numbers:

$$
1, \qquad 6, \qquad 11, \qquad 16
$$

These numbers are **congruent modulo** $\boldsymbol 5$ because they each have the same remainder $({\color{blue}{1}})$ when divided by ${\color{red}{5}}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =0\cdot 5+1 \\ 6 & =1\cdot 5+1 \\ 11 & =2\cdot 5+1 \\ 16 & =3\cdot 5+1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & ≡6 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 1 & ≡11 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 1 & ≡16 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 6 & ≡11 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 6 & ≡16 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 11 & ≡16 &  & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, consider the following list of numbers:

$$
2, \qquad 7, \qquad 12, \qquad 17
$$

These numbers are *also* congruent modulo $5$ because they each have a remainder of $\color{blue}{2}$ when divided by ${\color{red}{5}}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =0\cdot 5+2 \\ 7 & =1\cdot 5+2 \\ 12 & =2\cdot 5+2 \\ 17 & =3\cdot 5+2\end{aligned}
$$

We write this as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & ≡7 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 2 & ≡12 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 2 & ≡17 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 7 & ≡12 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 7 & ≡17 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 12 & ≡17 &  & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

To visualize congruence modulo $5$ more generally, let's write the sequence $0, \: 1, \: 2, \: 3, \ldots$ in a spiral around a circle so that each "layer" contains exactly $5$ numbers.

![](images/24/24c9af7d731f0be479f36367ce2e1deb0d2d691ffa575cfa843a1ca1742d2698.png)

Each "spoke" of our wheel contains numbers that are congruent modulo $5.$ Every number on a given spoke is congruent modulo $5$ to every other number on that spoke." :tutorial/id #uuid "079c66bc-ad87-56ed-85da-3ad13ba65bd5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9010 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "75bff31b-8ddd-5ea9-8a7e-ab19757aeb37" :step/math-academy-id 137420 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152917}} {:db/id 17592186152917 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153471 :tutorial/content "In general, two integers $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $n$ if and only if $n$ divides $(a-b).$ 

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b)
$$

We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

For example, the following numbers are congruent with respect to the given modulus:

- $6\equiv 1\:(\textrm{mod}\,5)$ because $5\,\mid\, (6-1).$ There is no remainder:

$$
(6-1)\div 5 = 5\div 5 = 1
$$

- $-2\equiv -8\:(\textrm{mod}\,6)$ because $6\,\mid\, \left((-2)-(-8)\right).$ There is no remainder:

$$
\left((-2)-(-8)\right)\div 6 = 6\div 6 = 1
$$

However, the following numbers are not congruent with respect to the given modulus:

- $6\not\equiv 1\:(\textrm{mod}\,4)$ because $4\,\not\mid\, (6-1).$ Note that $(6-1) = 5,$ which is not divisible by $4.$

- $0\not\equiv 13\:(\textrm{mod}\,12)$ because $12\,\not\mid\, (0-13).$ Note that $(0-13) = -13,$ which is not divisible by $12.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "30bcacad-ba7e-5d26-840a-8d0c84a74224" $$
(a-b) = (p-q)n.
$$

$$
(a-b) = kn.

$$
a = q{\color{red}{n}}+{\color{blue}{r}}, \qquad 0\leq {\color{blue}{r}} < {\color{red}{n}}.
$$

When two integers $a$ and $b$ have the *same remainder* ${\color{blue}{r}}$ when divided by ${\color{red}{n}},$ we say they are **congruent modulo** $\boldsymbol n,$ and we write

$$
a\equiv b\qquad  (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

The number $n$ is called the **modulus**.

To demonstrate this concretely, consider the following list of numbers:

$$
1, \qquad 6, \qquad 11, \qquad 16
$$

These numbers are **congruent modulo** $\boldsymbol 5$ because they each have the same remainder $({\color{blue}{1}})$ when divided by ${\color{red}{5}}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =0\cdot 5+1 \\ 6 & =1\cdot 5+1 \\ 11 & =2\cdot 5+1 \\ 16 & =3\cdot 5+1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & ≡6 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 1 & ≡11 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 1 & ≡16 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 6 & ≡11 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 6 & ≡16 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 11 & ≡16 &  & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, consider the following list of numbers:

$$
2, \qquad 7, \qquad 12, \qquad 17
$$

These numbers are *also* congruent modulo $5$ because they each have a remainder of $\color{blue}{2}$ when divided by ${\color{red}{5}}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =0\cdot 5+2 \\ 7 & =1\cdot 5+2 \\ 12 & =2\cdot 5+2 \\ 17 & =3\cdot 5+2\end{aligned}
$$

We write this as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & ≡7 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 2 & ≡12 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 2 & ≡17 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 7 & ≡12 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 7 & ≡17 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 12 & ≡17 &  & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
